overview: The atlas calls this century “Lambakannas,” a dynastic label. Evidence describes the late Anuradhapura kingdom, whose rulers are grouped in the Second Lambakanna line without reducing subjects to one dynasty or ethnicity. This keeps dynasty, kingdom, Sinhalese identity, archaeological sites, and modern Sri Lanka distinct. Its 900 to 1000 dates come from one atlas polygon, not regnal accessions or surveyed frontiers. It covers much of the island yet excludes Colombo, Jaffna, Trincomalee, and Galle; it is no survey. Inscriptions offer a richer view: royal titles and disputed ruler numbering sit beside village petitions, market tolls, tenants, householders, cooks, potters, painters, physicians, leech specialists, sweepers, laundry workers, teachers, and water distributors. Monasteries were economic institutions and religious homes. Their records describe scripture study, sick care, repairs, tanks, leases, wages, public accounts, and protections against official abuse. Evidence for children, women, and household privacy is thinner and often filtered through elite institutions. South Indian pressure intensified late in the period, but the atlas endpoint compresses an uneven political transition that continued beyond the card’s dated window.

periods.title: The atlas opens inside a disputed king list
periods.summary: An older sovereign table places Udaya I at 901 and Kassapa IV at 912, but it also prints alternative dates for nearby rulers. These boundaries are an editorial bridge from the atlas start, not proof that a coronation occurred at either edge of this band.

periods.title: A hospital village enters the record
periods.summary: A tenth-century Sinhala pillar gives its act as year eleven of Siri Saṅg-bo and protects a village belonging to a hospital on Anuradhapura’s High Street. Its editor argues for Kassapa IV, yet title-based identification makes the absolute reign an informed reconstruction rather than a certainty.

periods.title: Kassapa’s slab reveals institutional government
periods.summary: The Anuradhapura slab associated with Kassapa V records monasteries, medical halls, tanks, study, protection, and financial rules. Its direct evidence is stronger for institutions than for a modern reign chart, so this interval follows a conventional identification without pretending every title uniquely names one ruler.

periods.title: Dappula’s dating has two plausible tracks
periods.summary: The Kataragama pillar is in a sixth regnal year of Dāpuḷu, usually identified as Dappula V. The curated record gives about 946 if his reign began in 940, or about 924 under another chronology. This band displays the common reconstruction while preserving that substantial alternative.

periods.title: A damaged slab identifies Sena by elimination
periods.summary: Velmilla’s broken inscription names year eight of Mahasen Abhā. Palaeography, reign length, and the heir Udaya rule out two Senas, leaving Sena III as the editor’s attribution. The reasoning is explicit and useful, but it remains identification by elimination rather than a dated royal autograph.

periods.title: Numbering disagreements block sharp boundaries
periods.summary: Codrington’s older table assigns Udaya III to 964 while marking an alternative around 942 or 943, the same kind of displacement seen in the Badulla debate. This period is therefore a chronological holding band, not a claim that evidence suddenly changes in 964.

periods.title: Mahinda IV regulates Mihintale
periods.summary: Two 58-line Sinhala prose tablets state that Mahinda IV acted in his sixteenth regnal year. The curated record dates his reign to 975 to 991. Their detailed rules support a late-century institutional phase more securely than they establish every accession in the preceding sequence.

periods.title: Chola pressure reaches the atlas seam
periods.summary: UNESCO summarizes Anuradhapura as abandoned after an invasion in 993. A SOAS study instead structures Chola power through earlier relations, Rajaraja’s occupation of Rajarattha, and later consolidation and resistance. This final band marks mounting disruption; it does not turn one heritage date or the atlas endpoint into complete island-wide conquest.

sections.title: Read the label and polygon cautiously

items.text: The exact atlas id is lambakannas, with approximate dates from 900 to 1000, one observed border interval, and no prior summary, card, override, or staged draft. This packet researches that exact missing record rather than replacing the existing Simhala, Sinhalese kingdoms, Chola, or modern Sri Lanka cards.

The decoded target is one nondegenerate polygon with one ring and 35 stored positions, bounded roughly by 79.67 to 81.87 degrees east and 5.93 to 9.69 degrees north. Anuradhapura, Mihintale, Mantai, Polonnaruwa, Badulla, and Kataragama test inside; Colombo, Jaffna, Trincomalee, and Galle test outside.

At the 800 snapshot, the same tested interior places belong to sinhalese-kingdoms. At 900, they belong to lambakannas. This clean color change is an atlas relabel, not evidence that a new population arrived, a dynasty began exactly in 900, or the kingdom acquired a surveyor’s border overnight.

At 1000, the exact target vanishes and chola-empire owns all ten tested places that were inside the prior polygon. Madurai changes from pallava to chola at the same seam. The synchronized repaint exposes the source atlas’s broad periodization; it cannot establish one simultaneous conquest across Sri Lanka and southern India.

The Chola repaint persists at 1100, but the indexed Lambakannas layer ended a century earlier. “Lambakannas” is therefore interpreted as a dynasty-framed atlas label for the late Anuradhapura kingdom. It is not a synonym for every Sinhalese person, every archaeological layer, or the present-day Republic of Sri Lanka.

sections.title: Meet rulers without forcing false precision

items.text: The older sovereign table runs Udaya I, Kassapa IV, Kassapa V, two Dappulas, Udaya II, Sena III, Udaya III, Sena IV, Mahinda IV, Sena V, and Mahinda V across the century. Its own question marks and alternative dates show why those numbers should guide comparison, not become synthetic item years.

Kassapa V’s Anuradhapura slab survives at Abhayagiri and is linked to a published Epigraphia Zeylanica edition. The inscription records a ruler through titles and acts; its museum context and later attribution should not be confused with a complete palace archive or unquestionable accession date.

Badulla dates itself to year two of Siri Saṅg-bo Udā. Paranavitana identified Udaya III and obtained about 942, while other modern numbering calls the king Udaya IV and places him in 946 to 954. The secure statement is a mid-tenth-century charter; the ordinal and conversion remain contested.

Velmilla’s year-eight Mahasen Abhā is attributed to Sena III because Sena IV reigned too briefly and Sena V had a different heir. That transparent elimination is better than silent certainty. The damaged state, missing fragment, titles, and succession clues all belong in the historical conclusion.

Mahinda IV is unusually well anchored here: the Mihintale tablets name a sixteenth regnal year, while Siddham dates his reign to 975 to 991. Even so, the tablets describe one royal intervention in a monastery. They do not prove equal administrative reach in every region drawn inside the atlas polygon.

sections.title: Use law to limit officials and protect a market

items.text: Merchants and residents at Hopiṭigamu complained that officials had taken illegal fines, presents, and other exactions. The king ordered the earlier rules written down. Their petition shows subjects seeking redress through royal authority, while the public pillar turned a remembered rule into a durable and inspectable text.

The charter says royal agents should sit with counsellors, the merchant community, and village elders before imposing fines. That is evidence for negotiated local procedure, not modern representative government. A legal session joined royal, commercial, and village voices while still operating inside a ranked monarchy.

Siddham describes the Badulla text as a royal charter for mercantile corporations and says local merchant bodies could levy fines, arrest murderers, and assist royal officers with justice. These were delegated powers inside a monarchy, not modern civic equality; the record shows commerce and enforcement joined in village administration.

The Badulla rules bar visiting officials from demanding liquor, meat, curd, ghee, or toddy and from conducting illicit trade. They also protect pack bulls from seizure. A list of prohibited behavior is not proof that abuse disappeared; it is unusually direct evidence of what merchants and cultivators wanted stopped.

Goods sold in the market owed a toll, concealed sales could be charged double, and merchandise merely passing through was exempt. The distinction separates local sale from transit. Named officers later erected the pillar and complaints could trigger inquiry, making taxation, enforcement, publication, and appeal parts of one documentary system.

Kassapa’s slab credits the king with repairing monasteries, establishing royal medical halls, and making cultivation possible through the Podonavulu and Puluṇḍāvulu tanks. Court praise may magnify personal agency, but the combination shows that water storage, farming, religious patronage, and health institutions belonged to the same language of good rule.

The same regulations forbid officers to seize farm laborers, carts, oxen, or buffaloes from monastic villages and to cut their trees. These protections reveal the working assets behind cultivation. They also show that land grants mattered because people, animals, transport, timber, and official demands were entangled with the soil.

Mahinda IV’s Anuradhapura slab lets pamaṇu holders clear some forest land while restricting other allotment holders. Damaged lines describe tanks, ponds, cultivation, produce sales, and shares recommended by five village residents. Gaps in the stone matter: the edition supports structured resource rights, not a fully reconstructed agrarian code.

Later lines list betel, oranges, plantains, jackfruit, gardens, and possible well dues, then say tenants should not be ejected and allotment holders should do no injustice. The broken syntax blocks a universal tax schedule, but fruit cultivation, wells, tenancy, village judgment, and legal restraint remain visible.

Dry-zone water systems linked tanks, channels, fields, settlements, and rules for sharing labor and water. Modern research stresses that governance changed through time and differed by scale. This card therefore reads each inscription locally; it does not turn every reservoir inside the polygon into one centrally managed tenth-century network.

sections.title: Trade, cook, craft, and pay people

items.text: Chinese pottery found at Mantai and inland monasteries includes Tang and Five Dynasties material; a heavy glazed storage-jar type occurs only at the port and may have served aboard ships. Ceramics demonstrate long-distance contact, while their broad dynastic dates and possible gift use prevent assignment to one Lambakanna ruler.

An inscription-based food study lists boiled rice, gruel, green gram, curd, honey, butter, ginger, fruits, and other foods, often as offerings to monastic communities or care for sick monks. Its evidence spans the first through thirteenth centuries, so it supplies a comparative pantry, not a tenth-century household menu.

Siddham describes the Badulla charter as rules for Hopiṭigamy granted to local mercantile corporations and as evidence for tenth-century peasants and traders. That supports an organized inland commercial place, while the record still does not give prices, merchant household budgets, shop inventories, or the weekly purchases of ordinary residents.

Mihintale supported potters, an alms-bowl and water-pot maker, a water-strainer supplier, painters, thatchers, cooks, firewood carriers, carvers, bricklayers, woodworkers, lapidaries, blacksmiths, limeburners, cartmen, and laundry workers. Land, rice, cloth, or gold paid different roles, revealing an institution sustained by many specialized hands.

Gold kahavanu circulated broadly from the eighth through eleventh centuries. The official museum guide shows standing and seated figures and notes alternative readings of a Nāgarī legend. The wide date range prevents assignment to one ruler, but coin design and metalworking add another material form of value beside rice and land.

sections.title: Build religious institutions and keep them running

items.text: Kassapa’s slab says monasteries were rebuilt and five hundred monks established in residence. That round number belongs to royal commemoration, not a surviving census. More securely, the record connects kingship with physical repair, endowed communities, and a capital landscape in which large monasteries were enduring institutions.

The king is also praised for having Abhidhamma teachings written on gold plates and preaching in his own language. Gold publication is an elite achievement claim, while vernacular preaching points toward audiences beyond specialist textual study. The inscription celebrates both precious writing and speech as royal religious work.

At Mihintale, monks rose at dawn, cleaned their teeth, put on prescribed robes, recited protective formulas, and received gruel and boiled rice. Ill monks could be excused on a physician’s recommendation. This is a regulated monastic routine, not a timetable for every household on the island.

Mahinda IV’s Anuradhapura slab mentions the Daḷadā Māligāva, or Tooth-relic-house, and helped identify its ruined site southeast of the Thūpārāma. This ties an administrative text to a sacred building, while the surviving ruin and edited inscription remain archaeological evidence rather than a complete reconstruction of ceremonies.

Ritigala, Manakanda, Arankele, and Maligatenna preserve meditation-monastery landscapes spanning roughly the fifth through tenth centuries. They show that late Anuradhapura religious life extended beyond the capital’s enormous complexes. Their long archaeological ranges caution against assigning every path, platform, or repair to this single atlas century.

sections.title: See families, status, work, and young people

items.text: Mahinda IV’s Mihintale preamble names his mother, the anointed queen Dev Gon, as well as a royal line. Her appearance matters, but it comes through a male ruler’s pedigree and court claims about equal birth. One named queen cannot describe the work or choices of most women.

Mihintale officials took security from suitable householders for losses connected with receipts and payments. Elsewhere, ground rent applied to householders on monastic land but not to institutional serfs and employees. These clauses distinguish legal and economic statuses; “householder” is not a census category for one universal family form.

Badulla’s protection of wives and children from restraint shows a household master whose liability could threaten dependants. It does not reveal marriage age, household size, affection, inheritance equality, or children’s daily labor. Families enter this archive most sharply where officials might punish them for someone else’s debt or fine.

Kassapa’s rules say tender-aged youths should not be admitted into the monastic order. They also fund support for four destitute and four decrepit people. These narrow provisions reveal age and vulnerability entering institutional policy, while leaving childhood play, family teaching, disability, and care at home largely undocumented.

Mihintale names a monastery clerk, a registrar of caskets, and a keeper of caskets among officials receiving emoluments. These paid information roles reveal hierarchy and interdependence inside one monastery. Their titles document defined institutional work, not full biographies or evidence that every worker shared equal freedom.

sections.title: Study texts and read one secure sample

items.text: Mihintale assigned different food and clothing allowances to monks reading the Vinaya, Sutta, and Abhidhamma collections. This proves organized advanced study and material support within a monastery. It does not show universal schooling, literacy rates, a childhood curriculum, or that every monk followed the same educational path.

The same establishment supported a devotee who preached Buddhist doctrine and another who taught. Teachers and preachers appear beside florists, painters, and shrine staff, tying intellectual work to a wider payroll. The tablets document funded roles, not lesson plans, student ages, examinations, or ordinary village education.

Badulla’s complainants said an earlier rule had not been cut in stone, so the replacement decree was publicly inscribed. Written preservation mattered because memory and authority could be contested. The pillar is therefore both a legal text and a communication technology, although literacy among passersby remains unknown.

Secure written sample: “daḷdā-ge” appears in the scholarly Roman transcript of Mahinda IV’s tenth-century Sinhala inscription. The edition translates it “Tooth-relic-house.” The language is Sinhala and the historical writing was Sinhala script; the Roman letters shown here are transliteration, not the original letter shapes or a modern Sinhala facsimile.

Siddham says this 49-line slab uses the same style and language as the Mihintale tablets and was engraved only months later. That context securely dates the sample within Mahinda IV’s reign. No modern Sinhala glyphs are substituted, because normalized Unicode would look readable while falsely implying a facsimile of tenth-century forms.

sections.title: Treat medicine and sanitation as real institutions

items.text: A recent epigraphic study places hospitals inside Anuradhapura’s monastic economy, where grants, endowed resources, and care were linked. It identifies organized institutions without turning them into modern public hospitals. Surviving records illuminate patronage and administration more readily than patient numbers, access, diagnoses, or treatment outcomes.

The Kukurumahan-Damana pillar protects Kereḷǟ-gama, a village belonging to a hospital built by commander Gēna opposite the Mahindārāma nunnery on Anuradhapura’s High Street. It joins health care to endowed land and elite patronage. The editor’s Kassapa IV attribution depends on interpreting a recurring royal title.

A reused pillar found at Polonnaruwa records a freehold owing one unit of dried ginger yearly to a hospital founded by Doti Valaknä. The ruler could be Kassapa V or Dappula V. Ginger is an institutional payment here; the inscription does not say it treated every illness.

Mihintale’s tablets distinguish a physician and a practitioner associated with leech treatment, while broader epigraphic study connects healthcare to endowed monastic resources. These offices show organized care, not universal coverage or proof that every contemporary explanation of illness was medically correct. The record preserves staffing more clearly than outcomes.

A sanitation study describes stone urinals, latrine fittings, drains, baths, and water arrangements at elite monastic sites such as Abhayagiri, while warning that surviving remains favor privileged institutions and many structures resist precise dating. No selected source proves that an ordinary tenth-century household had a standardized toilet or sewer.

sections.title: End the card without inventing one collapse

items.text: A SOAS study treats Chola power as a sequence: relations before the tenth century, Rajaraja’s occupation of Rajarattha, Rajendra’s consolidation, and prolonged Sinhalese resistance. That structure resists collapsing invasion, capital movement, administrative change, and social continuity into a single event at 993 or 1000.

Specialist analysis says 993 is the earliest date when Chola inscriptions list Ilam among Rajaraja’s conquests. It also explains that the later chronicle never names Rajaraja and was compiled in the late twelfth century. Synchronizing inscriptions and narrative is necessary because neither source alone supplies a simple conquest timetable.

The same study separates Rajaraja’s foothold from later consolidation and examines Rajarattha’s administration and economy under Chola rule. Those are post-card developments, but they clarify the endpoint: military claims could precede fuller occupation, and changing rulers did not make cultivated land, institutions, or local society vanish.

The 900 polygon becomes a Chola layer in the 1000 snapshot and remains Chola at 1100. Those dates belong to the atlas file sequence. The geometry audit therefore records a repaint, while the historical card discusses the separately sourced 993 claim and post-1000 conquest process without treating pixels as primary evidence.

The atlas ends this id at 1000, while the Chola study follows occupation, resistance, and eventual reversal across much of the eleventh century. Political authority shifted in stages. The safe ending is transformation, with Mahinda V’s later capture, Chola consolidation, and continued regional life kept outside this card’s dated window.

ending.text: The 1000 endpoint is an atlas seam, not a securely dated extinction of the Second Lambakanna dynasty or the Anuradhapura kingdom. Chola conquest lists first include Ilam by 993, establishing a foothold before the seam. A later chronicle places a decisive invasion and Mahinda V’s capture in a regnal year often converted to 1017, but specialist analysis questions that number and points to earlier Chola temples and revenue assignments. The evidence supports stages: military pressure, territorial occupation, movement toward Polonnaruwa, later capture, and continuing resistance and local life. Anuradhapura’s royal role weakened, yet fields, tanks, religious communities, households, skills, and memories did not disappear together. The card ends with transformation and leaves successors empty because a generalized repaint cannot encode a trustworthy legal handover. Modern Sri Lanka, Sinhalese identity, the Chola empire, and archaeological Anuradhapura remain separate records and concepts.
